did_you_know.text: The Hebrew word “toledot” means not only descendants, but also the story or record of the generations that follow. This verse introduces the story of the human family.
In Hebrew, “adam” can mean both a specific person’s name and humanity in general. This verse connects these two meanings.

The phrase “in his likeness, according to his image” deliberately echoes the description of humanity’s creation earlier in the verse. The family list is therefore connected to the idea of the human image.
The letter samekh after the verse is a Masoretic sign marking the end of a reading section. It is not part of the biblical verse itself.
The name Enosh is related to the Hebrew word “enosh,” meaning a human being or mortal. The name itself reminds us that human beings are not immortal.
The name Mahalalel is probably formed from the words “praise” and “God,” meaning praise of God. Many biblical names include the word “El,” meaning God.
The name Jared resembles the Hebrew root yarad, which is connected with going down. The name may have been chosen because of this linguistic connection, although the verse does not explain it.
In the Bible, the phrase “to walk with God” describes a life of relationship, faithfulness, and upright conduct—not simply walking from place to place.
Enoch stands out in the genealogy: instead of the usual formula “and he died,” it says that he was no more because God took him. The verse leaves the manner of his disappearance mysterious.
Methuselah is the longest-lived person mentioned in the Bible: 969 years. He appears only in the genealogical lists of Genesis and Chronicles.

The name Noah is connected with the idea of rest, while the explanation “he will comfort us” adds the idea of consolation. The similar sounds create a Hebrew wordplay between his name and the hope placed in him.
